# Prime Numbers

Prime numbers are among the most fascinating and fundamental objects in mathematics. A prime number is a natural number greater than 1 that has no positive divisors other than 1 and itself. The first few primes are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23, and 29.

## Basic Properties

The number 2 is the only even prime, since every other even number is divisible by 2. This makes 2 uniquely special among primes. All other primes are odd.

The **Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic** states that every integer greater than 1 can be represented uniquely as a product of prime numbers (up to the order of factors). This makes primes the "building blocks" of all integers.

## Infinitely Many Primes

Euclid proved around 300 BCE that there are infinitely many primes. His elegant proof by contradiction assumes a finite list of all primes, multiplies them together and adds 1, then shows the resulting number cannot be divisible by any prime on the list — a contradiction.

## Distribution of Primes

As numbers grow larger, primes become less frequent, yet they never stop appearing. The **Prime Number Theorem** describes this distribution: the number of primes up to n is approximately n/ln(n).

Twin primes — pairs like (11,13) or (17,19) — are primes differing by 2. Whether infinitely many twin primes exist remains unproven.

## The Riemann Hypothesis

Perhaps the greatest unsolved problem in mathematics, the Riemann Hypothesis, concerns the distribution of prime numbers through the zeros of the Riemann zeta function. It remains unproven after more than 160 years.

## Applications

Prime numbers are not merely theoretical curiosities. Modern cryptography relies heavily on primes. The RSA encryption algorithm, which secures internet communications worldwide, depends on the computational difficulty of factoring large numbers that are products of two huge primes.

Primes continue to captivate mathematicians and inspire deep questions about the nature of numbers.

The sum 1+2+...+n equals n(n+1)/2. Pair the sequence with its reverse: (1+n), (2+n-1), (3+n-2). Each pair sums to (n+1), and there are n such pairs, giving n(n+1) total. Since we doubled the original sequence, divide by 2: total = n(n+1)/2.

This proof is attributed to Gauss, who as a schoolboy summed 1 to 100 by pairing 1 with 100, 2 with 99, recognizing each pair sums to 101, with 50 pairs, yielding 5050.

Since one of n or n+1 is even, n(n+1) is always even, so dividing by 2 yields a whole number.

Consider a right triangle with legs of length a and b, and hypotenuse c. The theorem claims the square built on the hypotenuse has the same total area as the combined squares built on both legs. This simple claim has profound consequences throughout mathematics, science, and engineering. Architects use it to verify corners are truly square. Navigators use it to calculate direct distances. Physicists use it constantly when working with vectors and forces. It quietly underpins an enormous portion of human knowledge.
